title: What If the Moon Disappeared Tonight?

props.earth: A single cute cartoon planet Earth seen from space, perfectly round, blue oceans and simple green continents, thick black outline, centered on a plain white background
props.moon: A single cartoon full moon, perfectly round, light grey with a few simple darker grey round craters, thick black outline, centered on a plain white background

locations.hill_night: A gentle grassy hill at night under a dark blue sky with small stars, a red and white checkered picnic blanket on the grass with a small wicker picnic basket and a small white telescope on a tripod next to it, a few round trees far in the distance
locations.town_night: A small cartoon town at night, a row of colorful little houses with glowing yellow windows, street lamps along the road, dark blue sky with small stars
locations.beach: A sunny sandy beach with a calm flat turquoise sea, a thin red and white striped measuring pole standing far out in the shallow water on the left side, a group of wet grey rocks with small tide pools on the right side, clear blue sky
locations.city_day: A cartoon city sidewalk in the daytime with small shops with plain blank awnings and no signs, green trees and tall buildings, clear blue sky
locations.reef_night: A colorful coral reef underwater at night, deep dark blue water, pink, orange and purple corals, some green seaweed
locations.cozy_room: A cozy cartoon living room at night with a wooden desk and chair on the left, a brown sofa, a bookshelf, a window showing the dark night sky, a warm lamp

location_props.hill_night: the red and white checkered picnic blanket with the small wicker picnic basket on it and the small white telescope on its tripod
location_props.beach: the thin red and white striped measuring pole far out in the water on the left and the grey rocks with small tide pools on the right, both well away from the characters

shots.text: At exactly nine P.M. tonight, the Moon disappears.
shots.scene: A small cartoon town at night under a huge bright full moon, houses with glowing windows
shots.anim: The full moon slowly fades away and vanishes from the night sky, the town stays still

shots.text: No explosion. No warning. Just... gone.
shots.scene: The same small cartoon town at night, the sky is completely empty with only small stars, no moon

shots.text: Within a day, the oceans stop acting normal.
shots.scene: (reuses shot 19)

shots.text: Within a week, baby sea turtles crawl the wrong way.
shots.scene: (reuses shot 87)

shots.text: And over millions of years, Earth itself could start to wobble.
shots.scene: (reuses shot 64)

shots.text: And Max is about to find out how much he needed it.
shots.scene: Max lies on a picnic blanket on a grassy hill at night next to a small telescope, looking up at the sky

shots.text: So what really happens if it vanishes? Let's find out.
shots.scene: Max and Zoe stand together on a grassy hill at night looking up at the empty sky, Zoe holds a glowing tablet
shots.anim: Zoe adjusts her glasses and looks up while Max scratches his head, gentle wind in the grass

shots.text: Max had planned the perfect night: a full Moon, a telescope, and his best friend Zoe, who just happens to be an astronomer.
shots.scene: Max and Zoe stand side by side on the picnic blanket next to the white telescope on its tripod, smiling and looking up at the bright full moon high in the sky, the picnic basket at their feet

shots.text: At nine o'clock, Zoe looked through the telescope, and the Moon simply wasn't there anymore.
shots.scene: Zoe stands next to the white telescope on its tripod with one hand resting on it, looking up at the empty night sky with a shocked open mouth
shots.anim: Zoe looks up from the telescope at the empty sky in shock, her mouth opens wide

shots.text: The first thing everyone noticed was the darkness.
shots.scene: A dark cartoon town at night with only a few street lamps glowing, deep dark blue sky with no moon

shots.text: A full Moon reflects so much sunlight that, on a clear night, you can see your own shadow.
shots.scene: Max stands on the grass beside the picnic blanket with both feet on the grass, the bright full moon high in the upper right of the sky, his long dark shadow stretches across the moonlit grass

shots.text: Without it, a moonlit night like that would become hundreds of times darker.
shots.scene: The same field almost completely dark, only tiny stars above, Max barely visible as a faint outline

shots.text: Within minutes, phones lit up all over the world.
shots.scene: A big cartoon city at night, apartment buildings with lit windows, a few stick figure people on balconies holding glowing phones
shots.anim: Windows in the buildings light up one by one as people look at their glowing phones

shots.text: News anchors stumbled over their words, and some people were sure it was the end of the world.
shots.scene: A cartoon TV news studio, a nervous stick figure news anchor in a suit sweating at the desk, a big screen behind him showing an empty night sky

shots.text: At observatories in New Mexico and France, scientists who bounce laser beams off mirrors that astronauts left on the Moon got a very strange result.
shots.scene: A white observatory dome on a mountain at night firing a thin bright green laser beam straight up into an empty starry sky
shots.anim: A thin green laser beam shoots from the observatory dome up into the empty night sky

shots.text: Their lasers never came back. The beams just kept going, out into space.
shots.scene: Two stick figure scientists in white lab coats in an observatory control room, standing at a desk and staring at a computer monitor that shows a flat empty line, looking confused

shots.text: But here's the surprising part: nothing crashed into Earth, and our planet didn't fly off into space.
shots.scene: Planet Earth calmly floating in space, the small bright Sun far away in the top right corner, no other planets
shots.anim: Earth slowly rotates in space, stars twinkle

shots.text: Earth and the Moon actually circle a shared balance point that sits inside the Earth itself, so our path around the Sun would barely change.
shots.scene: Simple cartoon diagram in dark blue space: planet Earth with a small glowing yellow dot inside it near its edge, and a dotted orbit path curving around a small Sun far away

shots.text: Zoe checked the numbers twice. We're fine, she said. For tonight.
shots.scene: Zoe holds a glowing tablet with charts, her face calm but serious, dark night background

shots.text: For tonight? Max asked. That didn't sound fine at all.
shots.scene: Max looks very nervous with a worried mouth and raised eyebrows, a drop of sweat on his head, dark night background
shots.anim: Max gulps nervously and a drop of sweat slides down his head

shots.text: The next morning, they drove to the beach. And something was definitely off.
shots.scene: Max and Zoe in a small red cartoon car driving along a sunny coastal road with the sea beside it
shots.anim: The small car drives along the coastal road, palm trees pass by

shots.text: The tide was supposed to be coming in. But the water barely moved.
shots.scene: Max and Zoe stand on a sandy beach staring at very calm flat sea water next to a striped measuring pole

shots.text: Here's why. The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans, stretching them into two bulges, one facing the Moon, and one on the opposite side.
shots.scene: Cartoon Earth on the left and the grey moon far away on the right in space, the blue ocean around Earth stretched into an oval toward the moon, curved white arrows showing the moon's pull

shots.text: As Earth spins through those bulges, most coastlines get two high tides and two low tides every day.
shots.scene: Cartoon Earth spinning in space with a curved rotation arrow around it, the grey moon far away on the right

shots.text: The Sun creates tides too, but its pull on our oceans is less than half as strong.
shots.scene: A big cartoon Sun on the far left edge and one much smaller planet Earth on the far right edge, a wide empty gap of dark space between them, the Sun and Earth do not touch or overlap

shots.text: So without the Moon, tides wouldn't vanish completely. They'd shrink to roughly a third of their size.
shots.scene: A cartoon beach with a wooden pier, old high water marks on the pier posts far above the calm low water

shots.text: That sounds harmless. Smaller waves, calmer beaches. Max actually thought it was kind of nice.
shots.scene: Max smiling happily, leaning back in a beach chair under a striped umbrella and holding a small cup, his two thin black stick legs stretched out in front, calm flat sea behind him
shots.anim: Max leans back in the beach chair and sips his drink happily

shots.text: And surfers? They would barely notice. Most waves are made by wind, not by the Moon.
shots.scene: Happy stick figure surfers riding big blue ocean waves on colorful surfboards on a sunny day
shots.anim: A stick figure surfer rides along a curling blue wave

shots.text: Then Zoe pointed at the rocks.
shots.scene: Zoe stands on a beach pointing seriously toward a group of wet rocks with small tide pools

shots.text: Tide pools, the little rocky worlds that fill up and drain twice a day, were drying out.
shots.scene: Close-up of rocky tide pools almost dry, a starfish, snails and a crab in a shrinking puddle under the sun

shots.text: Crabs, sea stars and snails are built for that rhythm. Change it, and whole shoreline ecosystems start to fall apart.
shots.scene: A sad cartoon crab and a sad starfish sitting in a tiny shrinking puddle on dry rocks
shots.anim: The sad crab slowly waves its claws as the little puddle shrinks

shots.text: Wading birds that feed on muddy flats at low tide would suddenly have far less to eat.
shots.scene: Several thin-legged wading birds standing on a narrow strip of mud by the sea, looking hungry

shots.text: Fishermen who plan their trips around the tides would have to relearn everything.
shots.scene: A stick figure fisherman in a small wooden boat scratching his head, holding a fishing rod, calm sea

shots.text: And tidal power plants, like the ones in France and South Korea, would lose most of their energy.
shots.scene: A cartoon tidal power station, a long concrete dam across a river mouth with turbines and power lines

shots.text: Even the deep ocean would feel it. Tides help stir cold deep water and warmer surface water together.
shots.scene: A cartoon cross-section of the ocean with swirling blue cold currents at the bottom and orange warm currents near the top
shots.anim: The blue and orange ocean currents swirl and mix slowly

shots.text: With weaker tides, that mixing slows down, and over time, ocean currents and weather patterns could start to shift.
shots.scene: Cartoon Earth in space with curved arrows on its oceans showing ocean currents and a few small storm clouds swirling over it

shots.text: Max looked at the flat, quiet water. Okay, he said. I take it back. This is not nice.
shots.scene: Max stands on the beach frowning at the flat quiet sea, arms crossed

shots.text: That night, Zoe took Max somewhere even stranger: a coral reef.
shots.scene: Max and Zoe snorkeling underwater at night with flashlights above a colorful coral reef
shots.anim: Max and Zoe swim forward slowly with their flashlights, bubbles rising

shots.text: Every year, a few nights after a full Moon, corals on reefs like Australia's Great Barrier Reef release billions of eggs at the same time.
shots.scene: A colorful coral reef at night releasing countless tiny pink and white eggs floating upward
shots.anim: Tiny pink and white eggs float slowly upward from the coral like snow

shots.text: It looks like an underwater snowstorm, and the timing is set by moonlight.
shots.scene: Wide view of a dark blue ocean full of tiny glowing pink dots drifting upward above the reef

shots.text: Without the Moon, corals lose one of their most important timing signals, and spawning could fall out of sync.
shots.scene: Pink and orange corals on a dark reef at night with small glowing question mark symbols floating above them

shots.text: If corals release their eggs on different nights, fewer eggs meet, and fewer new corals are born.
shots.scene: A few lonely tiny pink eggs drifting far apart in a big dark blue ocean

shots.text: On land, things got weird too.
shots.scene: A dark cartoon forest at night with many pairs of glowing eyes peeking from the bushes

shots.text: Dung beetles roll their little balls in a straight line by following moonlight and the stars.
shots.scene: A cute cartoon dung beetle rolling a round brown ball across sand under a starry night sky
shots.anim: The dung beetle pushes the ball forward across the sand

shots.text: On dark nights without that guide, they can end up wandering in circles.
shots.scene: A dizzy cartoon dung beetle on dark sand at night under a starry sky, a dotted circular path drawn around it

shots.text: Owls and other night hunters rely on the Moon's glow. Darker nights could make hunting harder for some, and hiding easier for their prey.
shots.scene: A cartoon owl on a branch squinting into darkness while a little mouse hides behind a rock below

shots.text: And some animals would actually win. Many small creatures are safer on dark nights, so their numbers could grow.
shots.scene: Cute cartoon field mice dancing happily together in a dark meadow at night, a few separate small moths flying above them

shots.text: Baby sea turtles hatch at night and crawl toward the brightest horizon, which is usually the open sea.
shots.scene: Tiny cute cartoon baby sea turtles crawling across a sandy beach at night toward the dark blue sea
shots.anim: The two baby sea turtles keep crawling slowly and steadily across the sand toward the water, both turtles stay the same size, shape and color the whole time, the sea stays calm

shots.text: On moonless nights, the glow of nearby cities could pull even more of them the wrong way.
shots.scene: Tiny cartoon baby sea turtles crawling up a beach toward bright orange city lights behind the dunes, away from the sea

shots.text: Nature isn't one big machine with a single off switch. It's thousands of rhythms, and the Moon is the drummer for many of them.
shots.scene: Cute cartoon forest animals, a fox, a rabbit, an owl and a deer, dancing in a circle around a drum kit on a forest clearing at night, the round grey moon glowing in the sky above them
shots.anim: The forest animals dance and hop around the drum kit, the drumsticks bounce on the drums

shots.text: Take away the drummer, and the band starts falling apart.
shots.scene: The same fox and deer from the reference image standing confused around the same drum kit in the same forest clearing, holding maracas, the night sky above is empty

shots.text: Back in the city, people were noticing other changes.
shots.scene: A busy cartoon city street in the daytime, stick figure people stopping to look up at the sky

shots.text: For thousands of years, humans have used the Moon to keep time. The word month even comes from the same root as Moon.
shots.scene: Ancient stick figure people in simple brown tunics carving crescent moon symbols into a big standing stone with simple stone tools, round straw huts in the background, night sky, no modern objects

shots.text: The Islamic calendar follows the Moon, and so do the Chinese and Hebrew calendars.
shots.scene: Three paper calendars hanging side by side on a plain wooden wall, each page covered only with rows of small grey circles showing moon phases, full, half and crescent, absolutely no numbers and no writing

shots.text: Ramadan begins with the sighting of a new crescent Moon, and Chinese New Year falls on a new Moon.
shots.scene: A stick figure family on a rooftop at dusk looking at the sky, glowing paper lanterns hanging nearby

shots.text: Without it, billions of people would need a new way to mark their most important days.
shots.scene: Planet Earth in space with a few small stick figure people standing on top of it looking up at the dark empty sky

shots.text: Max tried to lighten the mood. Good news, he said. No more werewolves.
shots.scene: Max grins and gives a thumbs up while Zoe stands next to him rolling her eyes, city street background
shots.anim: Max laughs and gives a thumbs up while Zoe facepalms

shots.text: Zoe didn't laugh. She was thinking about eclipses.
shots.scene: Zoe with her hand on her chin thinking deeply, a thought bubble with a dark circle covering the sun

shots.text: A total solar eclipse happens when the Moon slides perfectly in front of the Sun.
shots.scene: A bright yellow Sun in a dark blue sky with a dark grey disc sliding in front of it and covering most of it, a glowing white rim around the edge, a small town silhouette below
shots.anim: The dark disc slides further across the Sun until it covers it completely and the sky darkens

shots.text: With no Moon, there would never be another total solar eclipse, and no lunar eclipses either.
shots.scene: A small group of five stick figure people wearing dark eclipse glasses looking disappointed at a plain sun in a blue sky

shots.text: Space agencies would lose their closest target. Plans for Moon bases and new landings would be gone overnight.
shots.scene: A plain white rocket with an orange tip on a launch pad, the rocket has no face, three stick figure engineers in yellow hard hats standing next to it looking up confused at the empty blue sky

shots.text: Even the footprints astronauts left there in nineteen sixty-nine would be gone with it.
shots.scene: The grey dusty surface of the Moon under a black sky, a small white flag on a pole standing in the dust, a short trail of simple oval boot prints in the dust leading to the flag

shots.text: But astronomers would get one unexpected gift: darker skies.
shots.scene: Three stick figure astronomers standing next to white telescopes on tripods on a dark mountain top at night under a brilliant starry sky
shots.anim: Stars twinkle and a shooting star streaks across the sky

shots.text: Without moonlight washing out the sky, faint galaxies and the Milky Way would be easier to see every single night.
shots.scene: A breathtaking cartoon night sky with the glowing Milky Way band over dark hills

shots.text: Zoe smiled for the first time in days. It was the most beautiful sky she had ever seen.
shots.scene: Zoe smiling softly looking up at a sky full of stars and the Milky Way

shots.text: But for poets, painters and songwriters, the night sky would lose its most famous character.
shots.scene: A sad stick figure painter with a beret standing at an easel; on the canvas is a painting of a round grey moon; the real dark night sky above the painter is completely empty with no moon

shots.text: But the biggest effect of losing the Moon isn't something you'd notice in a week, or even in a lifetime.
shots.scene: Max and Zoe stand side by side on the picnic blanket, facing the viewer, both looking up at the starry sky with calm faces

shots.text: Earth spins on a tilted axis, leaning about twenty-three and a half degrees. That tilt is the reason we have seasons.
shots.scene: Cartoon planet Earth in dark space tilted to the right on a thin straight black axis line that runs through the north and south poles

shots.text: The Moon's gravity works like a hand steadying a spinning top, keeping that tilt from changing too much.
shots.scene: In dark space: a big cartoon hand coming from the left gently touching the top of a spinning top toy that has Earth's blue oceans and green continents painted on it, motion lines around the spinning top
shots.anim: The top spins steadily under the gentle hand

shots.text: Right now, Earth's tilt only shifts by about two degrees, over tens of thousands of years.
shots.scene: Cartoon Earth in dark space tilted on a thin straight black axis line, a small curved arrow near the north pole showing it wobbles only a little

shots.text: Without the Moon, many scientists think the tilt could drift much further, over millions of years.
shots.scene: Cartoon Earth in dark space leaning far over to one side on a thin black axis line like a wobbly spinning top, motion lines around it

shots.text: A bigger tilt could mean brutal seasons, with scorching summers and freezing winters.
shots.scene: A landscape split down the middle, the left half a scorching desert with a blazing sun, the right half a frozen snowy land

shots.text: Some regions could swing between ice and desert over long stretches of time.
shots.scene: A simple flat cartoon map of one continent seen from above, surrounded by plain blue ocean, white ice covering the top part, green land in the middle, yellow desert at the bottom, two curved black arrows between the ice and the desert

shots.text: There's one more change. The Moon slowly drags on Earth's spin, making our days a tiny bit longer every century.
shots.scene: Cartoon Earth in space with a simple round wall clock floating beside it

shots.text: Around four hundred million years ago, a day on Earth lasted only about twenty-two hours.
shots.scene: A prehistoric ocean scene with ancient armored fish swimming near the surface under a bright sun
shots.anim: Ancient armored fish swim slowly past

shots.text: Without the Moon, that slowdown would mostly stop, and our days would stay close to twenty-four hours.
shots.scene: The same planet Earth and the same round wall clock from the reference image, floating calmly in dark space

shots.text: Max did the math. So my great-great-grandkids might live through wild seasons, but they'd never get a longer day?
shots.scene: Max sits on a chair at the wooden desk with a notepad and a calculator, scribbles on the notepad, looking confused

shots.text: Pretty much, Zoe said. And no Moon to look at while they complain about it.
shots.scene: Zoe stands in the room smirking with her arms crossed

shots.text: There's an even deeper question. Some scientists think the Moon's strong tides may have helped early life, by washing coastlines back and forth between sea and land.
shots.scene: An ancient rocky coastline billions of years ago, shallow tide pools full of tiny green blobs of simple life, a huge grey moon low over the sea, no plants, no trees, no houses, no buildings, no people

shots.text: Without a Moon from the very beginning, life here might have taken a completely different path.
shots.scene: A strange alternate Earth landscape with weird friendly cartoon creatures with many eyes and long necks, no moon in the sky

shots.text: Some people believe the Moon protects us from asteroids, like a giant shield.
shots.scene: The grey moon in dark space with a glowing blue curved shield arc floating in front of it, small grey asteroids bouncing off the arc

shots.text: That's mostly a myth. The Moon covers a tiny patch of sky, so it blocks only a very small number of space rocks.
shots.scene: Cartoon Earth in space with a tiny moon far away and many small asteroids flying past on different paths

shots.text: Earth has been hit just as often. Our weather, oceans and moving crust simply erased most of the scars.
shots.scene: A heavily cratered grey moon next to a smooth green and blue Earth in space

shots.text: So could we survive without the Moon? Yes. Humans would be fine in the short run.
shots.scene: Max and Zoe walking side by side down a sunny city sidewalk, a few other simple stick figure people walking in the background

shots.text: But the world would slowly become a different place: quieter coasts, confused animals, new calendars, and an Earth that's free to wobble.
shots.scene: Three side-by-side picture panels: the left panel shows a calm empty beach with flat sea, the middle panel shows a small dizzy dung beetle on sand, the right panel shows planet Earth in dark space tilted with motion lines

shots.text: Max and Zoe climbed back up the hill where it all started.
shots.scene: Max and Zoe walk side by side across the grass toward the picnic blanket, smiling
shots.anim: Max and Zoe walk together toward the picnic blanket

shots.text: The sky was full of stars, brighter than they had ever seen. But somehow, it felt empty.
shots.scene: Max and Zoe sitting on a picnic blanket under an enormous starry sky with no moon, small figures

shots.text: You know what's worse? Zoe said quietly. This is the good version.
shots.scene: Max and Zoe stand facing each other on the grass in front of the picnic blanket, Zoe on the right talks to Max with a serious face, Max on the left listens with a worried face, both stand with both legs clearly visible, the picnic basket and the telescope stay behind them on the blanket

shots.text: If the Moon had exploded instead of vanishing, its pieces would still be up there. And some of them would be coming down.
shots.scene: The dark night sky over a small town filled with glowing broken rock fragments spreading out from one point where the moon used to be, there is no moon, only the broken pieces
shots.anim: Glowing rock fragments drift apart across the night sky

shots.text: But that's a story for another video.
shots.scene: Max staring up at the sky with a terrified open mouth and raised eyebrows, clutching the edge of the picnic blanket

shots.text: If you want to see what happens next, subscribe, and tell us in the comments what we should make disappear next.
shots.scene: Max and Zoe standing side by side smiling and waving at the viewer, plain light background
shots.anim: Max and Zoe smile and wave at the camera
